print_area._note: REAL print area, from Evan reading the Tapstitch editor 14 Sep 2026, replacing the placeholder canvas. editor_px is what the editor states and editor_dpi is the resolution those pixels are quoted at. 150 CONFIRMED (see below); it was also the only reading under which the design fits at all, since 150 was the only reading under which the design fits at all (at 300 the widest back area is 6.9in across and a 12in temple is impossible). It also lands within half an inch of the 14.98in area this catalogue printed on for a year. width_px and height_px are the editor numbers doubled, so the exported PNG is 300dpi at final size rather than 150; the aspect ratio is identical to the pixel, so 'upload, centre, full size' places it the same way. If the editor turns out to quote 300dpi, change editor_dpi and every inch in the layout halves: nothing else needs touching. CONFIRMED 16 Sep 2026 from Tapstitch's own API: the hoodie template's backSideDpiTip reads "Print area size 2067 x 2770 px (150)DPI", exactly editor_px and editor_dpi below.

front_print_area._ink_note: Both numbers are measured on the logo's ink, not its file frame. The logo PNG carries about 2.4% transparent padding across and 6.4% down, so the old frame-width rule printed a 5.86in logo where the config said 6.0in.

_naming_note: Was 'Pillar Temple Hoodie', then 'Cloud Temple Hoodie' from 16 Sep 2026, then 'Oversized Cloud Temple Hoodie' briefly the same day. EVAN, 16 Sep 2026: settled on 'Ultra-soft Oversized Temple Hoodie', leading with feel over the 'Cloud' brand word, matching the sweatshirt's new 'Ultra-soft Temple Sweatshirt' naming. Evan is updating the live Salt Lake City product's title by hand; this config only governs titles for every hoodie generated from here on. The rest of the 16 Sep reasoning still applies: this closes the 'whether the product line names carry over' question in BRAND.md section 7, and renaming costs nothing extra because a replacement never inherited its predecessor's web address by title anyway -- Shopify builds the address from the title, so the address is always set explicitly with productUpdate(handle:) after publish.

fulfillment._note: Evan, 14 Sep 2026: every line moves to USA fulfillment. Production 1-2 days and shipping 3-5 days, so 4-7 days to a customer's door against 10-17 from the international center. shipping_method is null because the US center's own service name was not read off the product page; the international options (Special Line, Special Line Pro, International Express) do not apply. Confirm the service name and the technique in the first editor session.
fulfillment._technique_note: DTF, not the DTG the RW0041 used. DTF lays a film layer on the fabric and gives strong opacity on dark grounds, which suits white line art, but large solid areas breathe less.

costs_usd._all_in_note: EVAN'S FIGURE, 14 Sep 2026, and the one to trust. Includes the blank, printing both sides, shipping, order insert, and payment gateway fees. No neck tag or hangtag (Evan confirmed 6 Oct 2026). Revised for USA fulfillment. The per-shipment line items that used to sit here were international rates and are gone rather than left to mislead; nothing below sums to all_in_per_unit.

_colorways_note: EVAN, 16 Sep 2026, chosen off real mockups. Six colourways, all US-fulfilled. SUPERSEDES a lineup that was STALE AND PARTLY IMPOSSIBLE: it listed 'Dark Gray' and 'Dark Green', neither of which exists on R00286 in any colour range. Those names belonged to the RW0041 blank this one replaced on 14 Sep, and the crew was updated for its own blank change that day while the hoodie was not. Verified against the live catalogue search, so every name here is one Tapstitch really has. Two are renamed on the storefront: Dark Purple shows as Mauve and Klein Blue as Royal Blue, driven by shopify_fixups.colorway_renames_by_type() from this table, which runs AFTER publish and must be re-run after any variant re-sync. CONTRAST, raised to Evan with the mockup: Dark Purple is RGB(178,156,175) and renders as a light dusty pink, so white art on it is the softest of the six, softer than the crew's Flower Gray. Kept at white deliberately; a black-ink version would be a separate product, because a Tapstitch template binds ONE design to a LIST of colour codes. COLOUR NAMES SPLIT 18 Sep 2026, Evan's call, and the reason is the theme, not the copy. shrine-theme-pro paints a colour swatch from ONE global list keyed on the option value NAME, so a name carries the same hex on every product on the store and nothing per-product can override it. The catalogue had three different greys and two names between them: the crew's Flower Gray #B4B3B5 (light heather) and the hoodie's Gray #6E7168 (warm sage) both published as plain 'Gray', and the tee's Dark Gray #56575B (cool charcoal) was a third colour again. Those hexes are the median fabric colour of the real Tapstitch mockups, print excluded, from artifacts/photo-mockup-spike/true_colors_all.json. Settled: crew -> Heather Gray, hoodie keeps Gray, tee -> Charcoal. The tee moved rather than the hoodie because a warm sage and a cool charcoal are genuinely different and folding either into the other would have put one swatch visibly off its own garment. Hex registry: config/swatches.json. Enforced at publish by scripts/swatches.py via finish_on_shopify.
_preview_color_note: Review-sheet background only, approximating Navy Blue, the colour this line opens on. Not a colour spec and nothing prints from it.
_spacing_note: Evan, 14 Sep 2026, superseding the earlier spacing: the temple and the location line are simply centred in the print file, vertically and horizontally, with the temple ink spanning no more than 12.0in at its widest point, the location line 0.7in of INK tall (not box), and the top of that line 0.5in below the temple's lowest ink. There is no top or bottom margin requirement any more, which is why both are 0.0 here: they were measured off the old back-stack layout, where the logo sat at the bottom of the back, and centring made them meaningless. They were also the only thing stopping tall temples reaching full width.
